intro: Miami's remarkable trees are mostly one man's doing and one forest's leftovers. Between 1914 and 1922 James Deering built Vizcaya on the Brickell Hammock, hoisting already large live oaks onto an artificial hill and buying more than a hundred Cuban royal palms, of which one survives. Simpson Park keeps 7.8 acres of the old hammock and a co-champion paradise tree. Further out stand a baobab in Miami Beach, a Coral Gables fig holding the last post of a packing house, and a champion false mastic near Homestead that was given up for dead after Hurricane Andrew. Only Vizcaya charges admission.
meta_description: Vizcaya's hoisted live oaks, the last of Deering's Cuban royal palms, and national champion trees in the Brickell Hammock.
question_answer: The oldest trees on this page are the Garden Mound Oaks at Vizcaya, four southern live oaks that Vizcaya's own label calls 200 years old, though a caption on the same page says 100. They were already large when they were moved onto an artificial hill built for James Deering between 1914 and 1922, so somewhere between one century and two is the honest range.
question_meta: Vizcaya's Garden Mound Oaks, 100 to 200 years old by Vizcaya's own captions, lead Miami's old trees. Where they stand and the rest of the list.
question_context: No tree on this page has been dated from its wood. The live oaks on Vizcaya's Garden Mound carry two ages from the same institution, 200 years on the mound's label and 100 in a video caption, and nobody has published a girth that would settle it. The estate's surviving Cuban royal palm is about a century old, worked out from the palm deliveries of 1916 to 1921 rather than measured. The champions are ranked by the Florida Forest Service on size, not years: the redberry stopper at Vizcaya, the paradise tree in Simpson Park, and the false mastic in Castellow Hammock near Homestead, which was thought lost in Hurricane Andrew and found alive in 1995. None has an age. Nor do the baobab in Collins Park, Miami Beach, or the Merrick fig in Coral Gables, which is on the map for the plantation post in its roots rather than its size. Vizcaya and Simpson Park are about two kilometres apart, and Vizcaya Metrorail station is about 500 metres from Vizcaya's entrance. If you know how old any of them is, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Miami?
faq.a: On this page, the Garden Mound Oaks at Vizcaya: four southern live oaks that Vizcaya calls 200 years old on one label and 100 on another. They were already large when moved onto the mound, built between 1914 and 1922.

faq.q: Are Miami's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Most are. Simpson Park, Collins Park in Miami Beach, the Merrick fig's street corner in Coral Gables and Castellow Hammock Preserve are free. The three Vizcaya trees need a ticket to Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, which is closed on Tuesdays.
A tropical hardwood forest on the Miami shore, of which Simpson Park keeps a 7.8 acre remnant. Vizcaya's own forest holds eight known national champion trees.

faq.q: How do I get to Vizcaya by public transport?
faq.a: Take Metrorail to Vizcaya station, about 500 metres, a five to ten minute walk, from the entrance.

trees.story:
This paradise tree shares the title of largest of its species in the United States. The Florida Forest Service lists it as a National Co-Champion: measured in 2009, it was 170 centimetres round, 16.8 metres tall and about 13 metres across the crown. Champion status is about size, not years, and nobody has dated it.

The setting is half the reason to come. Simpson Park is 7.8 acres of what remains of the Brickell Hammock, a scrap of tropical forest just south of downtown Miami, and the city's park brochure marks this tree as a stop on the numbered nature trail, labelled "Paradise Tree (Champion Tree)", behind the Charles Torrey Simpson Garden Center. The register's champion willow bustic grows in the same park.

One caution about which trunk. The register also lists a second paradise tree here, taller and thinner, still awaiting a verdict, and its own point for the champion sits about 100 metres from the brochure stop. Our pin is the brochure stop, so take the labelled tree on the trail as the one the city means.

Hurricane Irma stripped the hammock of its leaves in 2017, eight years after that measurement, and we have found no dated report of this particular tree since. The park is free, open daily from 8:00 to 17:00, with the east entrance closing at 16:00, and shut on holidays. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its place on the nature trail: the numbered stop the park brochure calls Paradise Tree (Champion Tree). It stands behind the Charles Torrey Simpson Garden Center building.

trees.story:
These four live oaks were already big trees when they were hoisted onto the top of a hill that had not existed a few years earlier. The Garden Mound at Vizcaya is artificial, built between 1914 and 1922 for James Deering's Miami estate, and Vizcaya's own account says the massive oaks were transported in and lifted onto it. A garden writer adds that they came from another Deering property.

How old they are depends on which caption you read. Vizcaya's label for the mound calls them 200-year-old, windswept live oaks; a video caption on the same page says 100. The garden writer says only that they were already large when moved, about a century ago. Nobody has published a girth that could settle it, so the honest answer is somewhere between one century and two.

What is certain is where they have spent the last hundred years: on an exposed hilltop in hurricane country. Vizcaya trims them regularly to make them more resilient when the storms come.

The four make a single stop. The mound sits at the south end of the formal gardens, up a short flight of stone steps, and the oaks are seen together from the top. Entry is paid, and Vizcaya opens Wednesday to Monday, closed on Tuesdays; check the hours before going. Vizcaya Metrorail station is about 500 metres from the entrance, a five to ten minute walk. Our pin marks the estate, not the mound itself.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by where they grow: four windswept live oaks on top of the Garden Mound, the artificial hill at Vizcaya. It stands at the south end of the formal gardens, up a short flight of stone steps.

trees.verify_notes: Register: circumference 53 in (135 cm) at 4.5 ft, height 57 ft (17.4 m), crown 22 by 14 ft, measured Dec 2013, National Champion by size (total points 115). Vizcaya itself names a Red Stopper champion, which is the owner-of-ground corroboration, but its caption does not say which of the several Vizcaya redberry stopper records (PK 10, 877, 895, 1023) it shows; 1023 is the only one currently titled National Champion, the others pending or emeritus. Slender hammock tree, remarkable as the largest of its species in the US, not for age. Weak page: no photo, no age.
trees.story:
The biggest redberry stopper known in the United States grows in the forest at Vizcaya, James Deering's estate in Miami. In December 2013 the Florida Forest Service measured it at 135 centimetres round at chest height and 17.4 metres tall, with a narrow crown about 7 by 4 metres, and named it National Champion for its species.

That is a claim about size. A stopper is a slender hammock tree, not a giant, and nobody has dated this one. Vizcaya, which owns the ground, is proud enough of it to caption a photograph "Red Stopper Champion Tree at Vizcaya", and says its forest holds eight known national champion trees.

There is a complication. The register carries several redberry stopper records at Vizcaya, and Vizcaya's caption does not say which one it shows. This record is the only one currently titled National Champion; the others are pending or emeritus. The measurement also predates Hurricane Irma in 2017, and we have not found a dated report of this tree since.

The stopper stands in the hammock, the forested part of the estate, on the register's coordinate, which we have not been able to tie to a particular crown. No source says whether the visitor paths reach it, so go knowing you may see the forest rather than the tree. Entry to Vizcaya is paid, and Vizcaya Metrorail station is about 500 metres from the gate. If you have found it on the ground, tell us where.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its build: a slender trunk about 135 centimetres round, rising some 17 metres to a narrow crown. It stands in the hammock forest on the Vizcaya grounds, not in the formal gardens.

trees.name: Vizcaya's Surviving Cuban Royal Palm

location.address: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, 3251 South Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33129

verified_sources: https://vizcaya.org/collections/gardens/about-gardens/ (fetched 2026-10-18: Deering purchased over one hundred Royal Palms from Cuba; 'One remaining palm is a Florida Challenger, the 4th largest Royal Palm'; palm delivery photo dated 28 Nov 1921)
Florida Champion Tree register, FeatureServer/0 OBJECTID 598 (PK 878), Royal Palm, Florida Challenger, Vizcaya Museum & Gardens, queried 2026-10-18

trees.transport: Vizcaya Metrorail station, about 500 m from the entrance.
trees.verify_notes: Register: circumference 60 in (152 cm), height 74 ft (22.6 m), crown 25 by 21 ft, measured Apr 2012, titled Florida Challenger, matching Vizcaya's wording. Not independently proven to be the same palm (Vizcaya gives no location), but only one Vizcaya royal palm record exists. Age: Vizcaya documents the Cuban palms arriving around 1916 to 1921 (dated delivery photo 1921) and says one remains; a palm of that planting is roughly a century, but the page does not state this specimen's year, so treat the range as derived from 'one remaining' original, not a measured age. Palm girth is a trunk circumference, not a tree-ring measure. Alive: Vizcaya's page (2025 items) still says it remains; register 2012; not tree-dated. Pin is the register coordinate, approximate.
trees.story:
James Deering bought more than a hundred royal palms in Cuba for his Miami estate. Vizcaya says one is left. Vizcaya publishes a photograph of a palm delivery dated 28 November 1921, and the shipments ran from about 1916 to that year, so the survivor has been standing here for roughly a century. That figure is worked out from the planting, not measured on the palm, and Vizcaya gives no year for this particular trunk.

It is also big. Vizcaya calls it a Florida Challenger, "the 4th largest Royal Palm", and the Florida Forest Service register agrees on the title: measured in April 2012, it stood 22.6 metres tall, with a trunk 152 centimetres round and a crown about 7.6 by 6.4 metres.

One honest gap. Vizcaya does not say where on the grounds its survivor stands, so we cannot prove the register's palm is the same one. It is the only royal palm the register records at Vizcaya, which makes it very likely, and our pin is the register's coordinate rather than a fix at the trunk.

The rest of the Cuban shipment is gone. Vizcaya's recent pages still say this one remains, though we have not seen a dated photograph of it. Entry to Vizcaya is paid, and Vizcaya Metrorail station is about 500 metres from the entrance.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height: a single trunk about 152 centimetres round rising 22.6 metres, the last of Deering's Cuban royal palms. It stands on the Vizcaya grounds near the register's pin, which is approximate.

trees.story:
Hurricane Andrew was supposed to have killed this tree. After the storm of August 1992 the false mastic at Castellow Hammock was thought to have perished, and it was dropped as National Champion of its species. In October 1995, a note by R. Hammer on its register record says, it was found standing, with some crown loss and otherwise in good health.

It has the title back. The Florida Forest Service lists it as the National Champion false mastic, and when the county forester, Mark Torok, remeasured it in January 2020 it was 279 centimetres round at chest height and 26.2 metres tall, with a crown about 15 by 11 metres. He recorded it as mature and healthy, the latest word on it we have found.

Champion means biggest, not oldest, and nobody has published an age. If you know one, tell us.

The tree grows in Castellow Hammock Preserve, 112 acres of Miami-Dade County parkland in the Redland, near Homestead, with a half-mile self-guided trail over uneven, rocky limestone. Entry is free. The county gives hours of 9:00 to 17:00 every day, while the Florida Birding Trail says Wednesday to Sunday, so check before you drive. You will need a car.

One honest gap: no source says whether the champion stands beside the trail, and the register's own coordinate lands on a road about 700 metres east of the preserve, so we do not trust it. Our pin marks the middle of the preserve, not the trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: 279 centimetres round and 26.2 metres tall, the biggest false mastic on the national register. It stands somewhere in Castellow Hammock Preserve; no source places it on the trail.

trees.name: The Merrick Packing House Fig

location.address: Castile Avenue at South Greenway Drive, Coral Gables, FL 33134
location.neighbourhood: Coral Gables (Country Club of Coral Gables Historic District)

verified_sources: https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=73634 (Historical Marker Database entry, 'Site of Packing House of Coral Gables Plantation', erected by the Gov. John West Chapter, Daughters of the American Revolution; read via Wayback)

https://www.coralgables.com/department/public-works/tree-year-contest/tree-year-submissions (City of Coral Gables Tree of the Year submissions, entries 'Merrick fig', 'Merrick Shack' and 'Merrick Post in the Fig', Centennial year 2025)
trees.access: Free. A public street corner on Castile Avenue where the marker stands; no entry needed.
trees.transport: Coral Gables, Castile Avenue at South Greenway Drive, beside the Granada Golf Course; no transit stop verified, writer must not invent one.

location_site.name: Castile Avenue and South Greenway Drive corner, marker site

trees.verify_notes: Historic rather than big: the point is the post. The marker text (HMDB transcription): 'Site of Packing House of Coral Gables Plantation, established by Rev. Solomon Greasley Merrick. Post in fig tree only evidence remaining.' HMDB marker coordinate 25 deg 45.001' N, 80 deg 16.303' W = 25.75002, -80.27172, 'at the intersection of Castile Avenue and South Greenway Drive, on the right when traveling west on Castile Avenue'. City nominations (resident submissions, edited by staff): 'the plantation's packing house is only survived by a single wooden plank, wedged between the aerial roots of a modest fig tree'; the Coral Gables Plantation was established 1906 by Solomon Merrick on grapefruit groves (a second nomination: Merricks bought 160 acres in mid 1899 for $1,100); one nomination says the shack was moved to that spot and used as an office for Merrick's plantation. Dates differ between nominations (1899 purchase vs 1906 plantation) and are resident statements, writer should use only the marker's words. Species: one nominator says Florida Strangler Fig, others only 'fig'; no authority names it, so genus only. Age of the fig: none published, do not derive. Alive: nominated in the 2025 Centennial contest; lifecheck NONE (no iNaturalist record nearby), thin, flagged. Pin is the marker; the fig stands at the marker per the marker text, not a surveyed trunk, so approximate with a 30 m site. A nearby tree is the Merrick House banyan (907 Coral Way, see leads), a different site.
trees.story:
All that is left of the Coral Gables Plantation's packing house is a wooden post inside a fig tree. The historical marker at the corner of Castile Avenue and South Greenway Drive says so in one dry line: "Post in fig tree only evidence remaining."

The Daughters of the American Revolution put the marker up. It records the packing house of the plantation established by the Rev. Solomon Greasley Merrick, then hands the rest of the job to the tree.

When Coral Gables ran its Tree of the Year contest for its centennial in 2025, residents nominated this fig three times over, as the Merrick fig, the Merrick Shack and the Merrick Post in the Fig. One nomination describes the packing house as survived by a single wooden plank, wedged between the aerial roots of a modest fig tree. Modest is fair. This is not a big tree, and it is on the map for what it is holding.

Which fig it is, nobody with authority has said. One nominator calls it a Florida strangler fig; the others say only fig, and so do we. Nobody has dated it either. If you know when it took hold, tell us.

It stands on a public street corner in Coral Gables, beside the Granada Golf Course, free to see from the pavement. The marker is on the right as you travel west on Castile Avenue, and the fig is at the marker. Our pin is the marker's position, not a surveyed trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wooden post wedged between its aerial roots. It stands at the historical marker on the corner of Castile Avenue and South Greenway Drive, on the right as you head west.

trees.name: The Baobabs of Collins Park

location.address: Collins Park, Collins Avenue at 21st Street, Miami Beach, FL 33139

verified_sources: https://communitynewspapers.com/miami-beach-news/miami-beach-sun-sand-surf-and-the-trees/ (City of Miami Beach piece, 11 May 2015, Urban Forester Mark Williams: 'a visit to Collins Park to see the majestic Baobab Tree should not be missed')
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/379173230 (iNaturalist, 2026-07-07, Adansonia digitata, 6 m accuracy, marked cultivated); 15 observations 2024 to 2026 in Collins Park
trees.access: Free. Collins Park is a City of Miami Beach public park beside the Bass Museum; open access (hours not fetched, writer must not invent any).
trees.transport: Collins Avenue at 21st Street, South Beach, beside the Bass Museum (2100 Collins Avenue); no transit stop verified on a transit page, writer must not invent one.
trees.verify_notes: Plural on purpose: iNaturalist observations 2024 to 2026 land at 25.7967 to 25.7973 and -80.1294 to -80.1303, an 80 m spread, so there may be more than one baobab and no source says which one the city's urban forester means. No girth, height or age found in any fetched source, so none recorded (a stock-photo caption mentioned 'hand carved initials' in the trunk, not fetched, ignore). Cultivated, not wild (iNaturalist marks the records captive), so it was planted; planting date unknown. A baobab outside Africa is the draw, in the words of the Urban Forester the tree is 'not just pretty, it also carries some lore. In some African cultures, the tree is considered the Tree of Life due to its strength and size.' Alive: iNaturalist record 2026-07-07 (research-grade neighbours, newest 2026). Source count: a city statement plus iNaturalist observations; flagged. Coral Gables has a separate baobab (6221 Leonardo St, nominated 'The Elephant's Foot', unverified, lead only).
trees.story:
Miami Beach's urban forester once told visitors not to miss an African tree. Writing for the city in May 2015, Mark Williams said a visit to Collins Park to see the baobab should not be missed, and gave it a line of lore: in some African cultures, he wrote, the baobab is considered the Tree of Life, for its strength and size.

It did not get here on its own. The naturalists who log it on iNaturalist mark it as cultivated, which means somebody planted it, and nobody has published when. Nobody has published a girth or a height either, so we can tell you what it is but not how big. If you know when it went in, or have put a tape round it, tell us.

The plural in our name is deliberate. Baobabs in the park have been recorded about fifteen times between 2024 and 2026, and those records spread across some 80 metres, which suggests more than one tree. No source says which one the forester meant. The newest record is from July 2026, so at least one is standing.

Collins Park is a free public park run by the City of Miami Beach, on Collins Avenue at 21st Street, beside the Bass Museum. We have not found its opening hours. Our pin is the middle of that 80-metre spread, not a particular trunk, so look for the baobab rather than the dot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the African baobab in Collins Park, an African species planted far from home. It stands in the park beside the Bass Museum, at Collins Avenue and 21st Street; there may be more than one.

trees.name: Fairchild's 1938 Baobab

location.address: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden, 10901 Old Cutler Road, Coral Gables, FL 33156

https://fairchildgarden.org/visit/tickets-hours/

trees.verify_notes: SOURCE: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden (owner of the ground) 'The Garden's Early Plantings' page: 11 tree species were planted by distinguished botanists at the inauguration on 23 March 1938 (article by Georgia Tasker, The Tropical Garden, 2013); of those 11 plantings only one survives, the baobab Dr David Fairchild planted, located near the Sunken Garden in the Montgomery Palmetum. The same page adds that the largest baobab in the garden stands near the NE corner of the Phillips-Atwater Gatehouse and was planted in 1938 from Dade County Nursery material. So there are TWO baobabs with 1938 provenance: the founder's tree (Sunken Garden/Palmetum) and the biggest one (gatehouse). Wikipedia (Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden) also says a giant African baobab collected and planted by Fairchild still grows there; A search snippet linking the Sunken Garden baobab to the 1927 Utowana expedition was NOT seen on a fetched page: not recorded. ALIVE: iNaturalist has repeated Adansonia digitata observations at one spot 25.6772-25.6774,-80.2755 on 2018-04-28, 2019-04-06, 2022-04-30, 2023-03-13, 2025-01-12 and 2025-06-07 (all casual grade, accuracy 4-8 m, so cultivated; not confirmed which of the two trees; the cluster is the best pin but it is not established that it is the founder's or the gatehouse baobab). Pin approximate at garden level, writer should say 'two baobabs, ask which'. No girth or height on any fetched page; do not invent. Commons has CC BY-SA 3.0 photo 'Adansonia digitata in Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden.JPG' (Nolege, 2011, not geotagged) as a pointer only; no photo hunt done. Single source (owner) per US rule: flagged 'one source'. Paid entry counts against the city's paid share (Vizcaya, Deering etc already heavy).
trees.story:
Eleven trees were planted at the opening of Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden, and one of them is still alive. On 23 March 1938, at the garden's inauguration, distinguished botanists planted eleven species of tree. The garden's own history of its early plantings says only one of the eleven survives, the baobab planted by David Fairchild himself, the plant explorer the garden is named after.

That makes it about 88 years old here, dated from the ceremony rather than from a seed, and the garden places it near the Sunken Garden in the Montgomery Palmetum.

There is a complication, and the garden supplies it. The same page says the largest baobab in the garden stands near the north-east corner of the Phillips-Atwater Gatehouse, and that it too went in during 1938, from Dade County Nursery stock. So the garden has two baobabs from its founding year, the founder's tree and the biggest one, in two different places. Our pin marks where naturalists have photographed a baobab again and again since 2018, but nobody has said which of the two that is. Ask at the garden which baobab is Fairchild's, and see both if you can.

A baobab is an African tree that stores water in a swollen trunk and drops its leaves in the dry season. Neither tree has a published girth or height. Entry to the garden is paid and it is open daily from 10 am to 5 pm, except on Christmas Day.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the swollen trunk of a baobab near the Sunken Garden in the Montgomery Palmetum. The garden's largest baobab, also from 1938, is a different tree by the Phillips-Atwater Gatehouse.

trees.story:
The big banyan in the Miami Beach Botanical Garden is older than the garden. Susan Askew of the Miami Beach Garden Conservancy, the nonprofit that runs the garden for the city, said in a 2022 interview that it is the only surviving original tree here. It was part of Carl Fisher's golf course, she said, and was likely there before that.

Fisher was the developer behind early Miami Beach, and this ground beside today's Convention Center was one of his golf courses. In the same interview Askew tells how he went bankrupt in the 1930s and the city took the land over. The garden grew up on it later, and the Conservancy has managed it since it was incorporated in 1997. Golf course, city land, garden. The banyan stayed put through all three.

A banyan is a fig from India that lowers roots from its branches. Where they reach the ground they thicken into new trunks, so an old tree slowly becomes a small grove of its own, standing on its own pillars.

How old this one is, nobody has said. Askew's account puts it on the site before the golf course and goes no further, and no planting date, girth or height has been published. If you know more, tell us.

Entry is free. The garden's own page gives different opening days in different places, so it is open most days, but check before you go.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the large banyan, the one tree the garden says survives from before it was a garden. It stands inside the Miami Beach Botanical Garden on Convention Center Drive.

trees.story:
Three hurricanes have knocked this baobab flat, and it is still growing, on its side. The National Tropical Botanical Garden, which owns The Kampong, says it was felled by Cleo in 1964, Wilma in 2005 and Irma in 2017, and that it now grows horizontally and thrives.

It started as a seed David Fairchild collected in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, on 9 April 1928. That makes it at most about 98 years old, counted from the seed. It was raised at the USDA's Chapman Field station in Miami and stood there until Cleo blew it down on 29 August 1964.

That should have been the end. Catherine Hauberg Sweeney, who had bought The Kampong the year before, rescued the fallen tree and had it planted here, which the garden believes was likely the first time a mature baobab that size had been transplanted. In October 2005 Wilma pushed it over again, and staff, volunteers, tree climbers, a backhoe and the largest crane that would fit put it back. Afterwards, by the garden's account, it dropped its leaves for only about half its old eight to ten weeks and fruited more than before. In September 2017 Irma brought it down a third time, toppled by other trees falling onto it. Today, the garden says, it grows lying down.

No girth or height has been published, and the garden has not placed it on a map, so ask for it when you arrive. Entry is paid, Tuesday to Saturday.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big baobab lying on its side and still growing, the one the garden says three hurricanes brought down. It lies somewhere in The Kampong's grounds, so ask the staff to point you to it.

trees.story:
The big banyan at the entrance to Bayside Marketplace has no official paperwork at all. We found no city tree record and no news story about it, and the marketplace's encyclopedia entry never mentions it. What it has instead is a crowd of witnesses. Naturalists have logged a banyan on this spot again and again since 2023, most recently in 2026, their GPS fixes agreeing to within about 15 metres, and a visitor recorded it as an exceptional tree back in 2010.

That visitor also wrote down a height and an age. Nothing behind either figure has turned up, so we leave both out rather than pass them on as fact. If you know when this tree was planted, or what stood here before the marketplace, tell us.

What you can check for yourself is a big banyan with aerial roots, standing on the downtown waterfront beside Bayfront Park. The species is the national tree of India, where a single old banyan can spread on its prop roots until it covers the ground of a small wood.

It costs nothing to see and it needs no car. Metromover stops serve Bayfront Park, a few minutes' walk away, and the tree stands on the public walkway rather than inside the shops.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big banyan with aerial roots at the Bayside Marketplace entrance, on the public waterfront walkway at 401 Biscayne Boulevard, beside Bayfront Park.
